title: Why does an application report "connection pool exhausted" while the database sits mostly idle (connections held by long/idle-in-transaction sessions, often an external call made inside a transaction), and how does `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` help?
shortTitle: Why does an app report "connection pool exhausted" while the database sits mostly idle?
keyPoints: A pooled connection counts as 'in use' from borrow to return, regardless of whether the database is executing a query.
The classic cause is an external HTTP call made inside a `@Transactional` method, holding the connection idle for the duration of the network call.
PostgreSQL shows these sessions as 'idle in transaction' in `pg_stat_activity`, which is the diagnostic signature.
The `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` setting automatically aborts transactions idle too long, freeing the connection and surfacing the bug.
The real fix is architectural: never make external calls inside a transaction; restructure so the transaction does only database work and commits quickly.
Other causes include forgotten connection closes (leaks), long-running reports holding connections, and missing commit/rollback on error paths.
Setting both a `statement_timeout` and a `leakDetectionThreshold` catches slow queries and leaked connections as additional safety nets.

s1_definition.oneliner: The pool empties because connections are held inside open transactions waiting on slow non-database work; `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` kills those stuck transactions and frees the connections.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **The paradox** – Pool exhaustion with an idle database happens when borrowed connections are held open but not doing database work, so the pool empties while the database has nothing to execute.
- **Classic cause** – A connection kept inside an open transaction while the thread waits on an external HTTP call inside a `@Transactional` method.
- **Diagnostic** – PostgreSQL shows these sessions as `idle in transaction` in `pg_stat_activity`.
- **Safety net** – `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` automatically aborts a transaction idle too long, releasing the connection and turning a silent hang into a loud error.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India has three ledger phone lines. A teller picks up a line to start recording Rajesh's loan, but mid-way they put the ledger clerk on hold and walk off to phone an outside credit bureau that takes thirty seconds to answer. The ledger clerk sits idle, the line is tied up, and soon all three lines are held by tellers waiting on outside calls. Customers queue and get 'all lines busy,' yet the ledger room is silent because no actual recording is happening.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The paradox of a pool reporting exhaustion while the database sits idle is explained by one fact: a pooled connection counts as in use from the moment you borrow it until you return it, whether or not the database is executing anything. If connections are held open but doing no database work, the pool drains while the database CPU stays near zero. That signature: pool timeout errors with a calm database: points almost always at one root cause: slow, non-database work being done inside an open transaction.

The classic offender is an external HTTP call made inside a `@Transactional` method. Spring opens a transaction on a pooled connection at the start of the method and holds it until the method returns. If the method calls a credit bureau or a payment gateway that takes several seconds, the connection is pinned for that whole time while the database does nothing. Under load, every request pins a connection for the external call, the pool empties, and new requests block and time out. PostgreSQL shows these as `idle in transaction` in `pg_stat_activity`, which is the diagnostic.

The `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` setting is the safety net. It tells PostgreSQL to abort any transaction that has been idle beyond the timeout, freeing the server side, releasing locks, and turning a silent hang into a loud error that points at the bug. But it is a safety net, not a cure. The real fix is architectural: never make an external call inside a transaction. Restructure so the slow call happens outside the transaction boundary and the transaction does only database work and commits in milliseconds.

At the National Bank of India, the loan approval service was exhausting its pool because the credit bureau call sat inside the transaction. Rajesh moved the call outside, kept the transaction to just the two fast database operations, and set an idle-in-transaction timeout and a statement timeout as safety nets. The pool stayed healthy even under heavy load.

Remember one sentence: the pool empties because connections are held inside open transactions waiting on slow non-database work, and the fix is to keep transactions short and database-only.
